title: FlyDubai Co-Pilot Who Attempted Mid-Air Attack Had History of Extremist Red Flags, Sources Say
snippet: Investigators are probing the background of the FlyDubai co-pilot who tried to crash a flight bound for Tel Aviv, revealing he was previously flagged for radical behavior at another airline.
content:
Terrifying details are emerging about the co-pilot accused of trying to violently bring down a FlyDubai passenger jet bound for Tel Aviv, as intelligence sources reveal the suspect had a history of extremist behavior that went unvetted prior to his hiring.

According to sources familiar with the investigation, the co-pilot has been identified as Hamam al Hamami, an Omani citizen raised largely abroad. The harrowing incident unfolded aboard a flight carrying 174 people from Dubai to Israel when al Hamami allegedly stabbed the captain and attempted to sabotage the plane's controls in what officials suspect was an attempted suicide crash.

Despite his injuries, the captain managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to intervene. Passengers tackled the suspect while two off-duty pilots aboard the flight took over the controls, successfully diverting the plane to an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. While no passengers were critically hurt, the captain and two crew members suffered injuries.

Unheeded Warning Signs

Intelligence sources revealed that al Hamami previously worked for Oman Air, where government surveillance caught him browsing radical websites while in pilot training. Oman Air subsequently stripped him of his flying duties and placed him in an office role, from which he eventually resigned around 2024.

Sources also noted that al Hamami had previously posted a video online depicting El Al Israeli Airlines aircraft alongside an image of slain al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri. Despite these prominent red flags, FlyDubai reportedly hired al Hamami without consulting Omani authorities or conducting a thorough background check.

Terror Probe and International Interrogation

Authorities in multiple countries are treating the mid-air attack as a potential act of terrorism. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed that evidence points toward rapid Islamist radicalization, noting that investigators are working to determine if the suspect acted alone or was directed by an extremist group.

"He came to crash the plane with its passengers," Netanyahu said in a statement, warning that any group found responsible would pay a steep price. Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump publicly raised the possibility of Iranian involvement, though Israeli officials stated it is too early to draw definitive conclusions regarding foreign state sponsorship.

Following his arrest by Saudi forces, al Hamami was transferred to the United Arab Emirates. He is currently being interrogated by a joint team of Emirati, Saudi, and Israeli intelligence officials as the multi-nation investigation continues.
